newsitem.title: FRANCE: Woman wins French literary prize with first novel.
newsitem.headline: Woman wins French literary prize with first novel.

text.p: French writer Pascale Roze won the Goncourt prize, France's top literary award, on Tuesday for her first novel "Chasseur Zero" (Zero Hunter).
The prize for a work of fiction in French is given annually at a gourmet lunch in Paris by 10 leading literary personalities.

The book, about a woman who investigates the death of her father at the hands of a young Japanese kamikaze pilot, won the prize at the third ballot, jury president Dider Decoin told reporters in a statement carried live by French television.
An earlier ballot had split the jury five for and five against "Rhapsodie Cubaine" (Cuban Rhapsody) by Cuban-born French national Eduardo Manet.

The Goncourt prize, founded in 1903, is formally worth just 50 francs ($10) but it promises a jump in book sales. Last year's winner, "Le Testament Francais" (The French Will) by Russian-born writer Andrei Makine has sold 520,000 copies.

The literary season kicked off last week when the Femina prize was awarded to French writer Genevieve Brisac for "Un Weekend de Chasse a la Mere" (A Weekend Hunting Mother), the tragic tale of a single mother fighting for custody of her son.
